content: 1. Venturi V, Tridapalli E, Sandri F, et al. conducted a study on the use of cranial ultrasound scanning to predict outcomes in newborns with congenital cytomegalovirus infection. This research was published in The Journal of Pediatrics in 2007, volume 150, issue 2, pages 157-161. 2. La Piana R, Uggetti C, Roncarolo F, Vanderver A, Olivieri I, Tondu T, et al. described neuroradiologic patterns and novel imaging findings in Aicardi-Goutières syndrome. Their findings were published in Neurology in 2016, volume 86, issue 1, pages 28-35. 3. O'Driscoll MC, Daly SB, Urquhart JE, Black GC, Pilz DT, Brockmann K, et al. identified that recessive mutations in the gene encoding the tight junction protein occludin result in band-like calcification, simplified gyration, and polymicrogyria. This study appeared in American Journal of Human Genetics in 2010, volume 87, issue 3, pages 354-364. 4. Besnard M, Lastere S, Teissier A, Cao-Lormeau V, and Musso D provided evidence of perinatal transmission of the Zika virus in French Polynesia between December 2013 and February 2014. Their findings were published in Euro Surveillance in 2014, volume 19, issue 13. 5. Cordeiro MT, Pena LJ, Brito CA, Gil LH, and Marques ET reported the presence of positive IgM for Zika virus in the cerebrospinal fluid of 30 neonates with microcephaly in Brazil. This study was published in The Lancet in 2016, volume 387, issue 10030, pages 1811-1812. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines on neonatal seizures in 2011, which are accessible online. These guidelines provide recommendations for the management of neonatal seizures. 7. The WHO also released a document in 2016 titled Pediatric Emergency Triage, Assessment, and Treatment: Care of Critically Ill Children, which outlines protocols for managing critically ill pediatric patients, including those exposed to Zika virus in utero. 8. The WHO's 2010 mhGAP Intervention Guide provides evidence-based recommendations for mental health care, including for neonates and infants with complications related to Zika virus exposure. 9. The WHO's 2010 Community-Based Rehabilitation Guidelines offer strategies for supporting individuals with disabilities, including those with neurological complications. 10. In 2016, the WHO issued interim guidance for healthcare providers on psychosocial support for pregnant women and families affected by microcephaly and other neurological complications associated with Zika virus. 11. Harris SR updated the methodology for measuring head circumference in infants with microcephaly in a 2015 article published in Canadian Family Physician, volume 61, issue 8, pages 680-684. 12. Bale JF, Miner L, and Petheram SJ reviewed congenital cytomegalovirus infection in a 2002 article in Current Treatment Options in Neurology, volume 4, issue 3, pages 225-230. 13. Ivarsson SA, Lernmark B, and Svanberg L conducted a ten-year follow-up study on children with congenital cytomegalovirus infection who did not exhibit neurological symptoms at one year of age. This study was published in Pediatrics in 1997, volume 99, issue 6, pages 800-803. 14. Lombardi G, Garofoli F, and Stronati M reviewed the treatment, sequelae, and follow-up of congenital cytomegalovirus infection in a 2010 article in the Journal of Maternal-Fetal and Neonatal Medicine, volume 23, supplement 3, pages 45-48. 15. The American Academy of Pediatrics Joint Committee on Infant Hearing released a position statement in 2007 outlining principles and guidelines for early hearing detection and intervention programs. This was published in Pediatrics, volume 120, issue 4, pages 898-921. 16.
